newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines ponders who will be next president.
newsitem.headline: Philippines ponders who will be next president.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court on Wednesday basked in rare praise after it effectively barred President Fidel Ramos from running for a second term, but left the country worried about who could replace him.
The Court on Tuesday surprised many by upholding its earlier decision to bar a petition to change the 10-year old constitution to allow Ramos to run in the 1998 presidential election.

"This is a welcome development. The issue of extending the tenure of President Ramos has started to polarise the people and threatens to adversely affect his effectiveness as head of state," the Manila Standard said in an editorial.
The constitution, written in 1987 after the 20-year hardline rule of Ferdinand Marcos had collapsed, limits presidents to one six-year term.
The response on the stock market was immediately positive, dispelling some recent bearishness over the economy. The main index in Manila opened 0.22 points higher on Wednesday at 2,775.33.
"It's contributing to the market...since it means there's political stability," said Elline Salvatierra, analyst at Dharmala Securities.
She added that had the Supreme Court gone the other way, prices could have fallen sharply on fears of instability in the country.
For the Supreme Court, which has been hammered recently by charges of corruption, it was a change to receive so much praise and a number of editorials hailed it for a brave decision.
Now the race is on to replace Ramos, whose five years in power has been credited with turning the Philippines from the "sick man of Asia" to one of the region's most vibrant economies.
Economic analysts, though they admit they will miss Ramos, say the outcome was probably for the best.

"Most people I talk to would have preferred if President Ramos stayed...but getting to that point would have been messy and unstable. It's better that we stick to the game plan," director of Socgen-Crosby UBP Securities, Roman Azanza, said.
The question now is who will take his place from the dozen or so aspirants already trying to make their mark.
"The awful truth, viewing the aspirants and wannabes already shadow-boxing, is that we're not faced with any happy choices," publisher of the Philippine Star Max Soliven said.
Few candidates stand out as obvious choices.
A group of some opposition parties were due later in the day to join forces and most likely select vice-president Joseph Estrada as their candidate.
The former movie star commands a large following among the masses but is generally distrusted by the business community.
Analysts say the most powerful candidate could well be the one picked by Ramos, but the current president is unlikely to make his choice known until much later in the year.
